content_voiceover: This flowchart from Blood 2014 outlines a practical strategy for managing DOAC associated bleeding, and it starts with risk stratification into minor, moderate, or severe and life threatening bleeding. For minor bleeding, local hemostatic measures are usually sufficient, and clinicians should consider whether to withhold the anticoagulant, weighing thrombotic risk against bleeding risk on a case by case basis. For moderate bleeding, general measures include withdrawing the anticoagulant, applying mechanical compression, closely monitoring hemodynamic status, giving volume replacement, and pursuing definitive interventions like endoscopy when indicated, alongside targeted blood product transfusion, red cells for anemia, plasma for coagulopathy such as DIC or dilutional coagulopathy, and platelets if the patient is also on an antiplatelet agent. Severe or life threatening bleeding escalates care to an intensive care setting with hemodynamic support, and clinicians should consider prothrombin complex concentrate, either four factor PCC at fifty units per kilogram or activated PCC at eighty units per kilogram. Adjunctive therapies at this stage include oral activated charcoal if dabigatran was ingested within the past two hours, hemodialysis for dabigatran removal since it has relatively low protein binding, desmopressin, and antifibrinolytic agents like tranexamic acid.
keypoints: Bleeding management starts with risk stratification into minor, moderate, or severe
Moderate bleeding combines general supportive measures with targeted blood product transfusion
Severe bleeding may require four factor or activated PCC in an ICU setting
Dabigatran can be removed by hemodialysis or bound by charcoal after recent ingestion
